content.title: ESC Guidelines
content.narrative_summary: This page provides the preamble to the ESC Guidelines, explaining that guidelines summarize and evaluate evidence to assist health professionals in management decisions while emphasizing that final decisions for individual patients rest with the responsible clinician. It describes the process of guideline development by the European Society of Cardiology, including the establishment of quality criteria, the use of registries, educational materials, selection of Task Force members, evidence review, grading of recommendations, conflict of interest declarations, and approval by the Committee for Practice Guidelines.

content.narrative_summary: The Introduction outlines the prevalence and management of supraventricular tachycardias (SVTs), the history of the 2003 ESC and US guidelines, and the formation of a Task Force to update evidence-based recommendations. Section 2.1 describes the literature review process, grading of evidence, and peer review. Section 2.2 details ESC policy on sponsorship, volunteer writing groups, and conflict of interest disclosures. Section 2.3 notes that many therapies from 2003 are no longer recommended or have changed in the 2019 update, with specific changes summarized in Table 3.

content.narrative_summary: Section 2.3.3 outlines new revised concepts including drug therapy for inappropriate sinus and focal atrial tachycardia; therapeutic options for acute conversion and anticoagulation of atrial flutter; therapies for atrioventricular nodal and antidromic atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardias including pre-excited atrial fibrillation; management of asymptomatic pre-excitation; and diagnosis and therapy of tachycardiomyopathy. Section 3 begins the definitions and classification of SVT, defining SVT as atrial rates >100 b.p.m. at rest with mechanisms involving tissue from the His bundle or above.

rows.recommendation: i.v. amiodarone is not recommended for pre-excited AF.
Performance of an EPS to risk-stratify individuals with asymptomatic pre-excitation should be considered.

Catheter ablation is recommended in asymptomatic patients in whom electrophysiology testing with the use of isoprenaline identifies high-risk properties, such as SPERRI ≤250 ms, AP ERP ≤250 ms, multiple APs, and an inducible AP-mediated tachycardia.
Non-invasive evaluation of the conducting properties of the AP in individuals with asymptomatic pre-excitation may be considered.
Catheter ablation may be considered in a patient with asymptomatic pre-excitation and low-risk AP at invasive or non-invasive risk stratification.
Catheter ablations should be considered in patients with asymptomatic pre-excitation and LV dysfunction due to electrical dyssynchrony.
AV nodal ablation with subsequent pacing (‘ablate and pace’), either biventricular or His-bundle pacing, is recommended if a tachycardia responsible for TCM cannot be ablated or controlled by drugs.
During the first trimester of pregnancy, it is recommended that all antiarrhythmic drugs are avoided, if possible.
In pregnant women, beta-1 selective blockers (except atenolol) or verapamil, in order of preference, should be considered for prevention of SVT in patients without WPW syndrome.
In pregnant women, flecainide or propafenone should be considered for prevention of SVT in patients with WPW syndrome and without ischaemic or structural heart disease.

content.narrative_summary: The page presents two classification tables: Table 5 categorizes supraventricular tachycardias into atrial tachycardias (sinus, focal, multifocal, macro-re-entrant [cavotricuspid and non-cavotricuspid], and atrial fibrillation) and AV junctional tachycardias (AVNRT, non-re-entrant junctional tachycardia, and AVRT). Following the tables, prose notes that SVTs may manifest as narrow or wide QRS rhythms and that AF is excluded from these guidelines. The new section on electrophysiological mechanisms introduces abnormal impulse initiation by enhanced automaticity and the concept of re-entry, with detailed circuit schematics in the Supplementary Data.

content.narrative_summary: This page introduces anatomical considerations for the electrophysiologist (section 5), presents epidemiological data on supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) including prevalence, gender and age differences, common substrates such as AVNRT, AVRT, and WPW pattern, and outcomes of catheter ablation (section 6). The section’s narrative ends mid-discussion of re-entrant tachycardias.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Initial evaluation of the patient with supraventricular tachycardia
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Standard evaluation includes: history, physical examination, and 12-lead ECG; full blood counts, biochemistry profile, and thyroid function; an ECG during tachycardia should be sought; transthoracic echocardiography. Optional evaluation includes: exercise tolerance testing; 24 h ECG monitoring, transtelephonic monitoring, or an implantable loop recorder; myocardial ischaemia testing in patients with risk factors for coronary artery disease (including men aged >40 years and post-menopausal women); an EPS for definitive diagnosis and when catheter ablation is anticipated.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues the discussion of initial evaluation of patients with supraventricular tachycardia, emphasizing comprehensive history (including family history), physical examination, and the importance of ECG documentation. It describes re-entrant arrhythmia clues from onset/termination patterns, vagal maneuvers and drug administration for diagnosis, and the role of blood tests, biochemistry, renal and thyroid function, echocardiography, and ambulatory monitoring (including 12-lead ECG, 24-h recordings, implantable loop recorders, and wearable devices). Exercise testing, ischaemia evaluation in angina cases, and electrophysiology studies when ablation is anticipated are also noted. Section 9 introduces the differential diagnosis of narrow QRS tachycardias (<120 ms) via His–Purkinje system activation. It outlines ECG criteria for distinguishing SVT from VT in sinus rhythm, discusses the presence or absence of pre-excitation in AVRT, and highlights the value and limitations of ECG during tachycardia. Subsections cover initiation/termination patterns (warm-up and cool-down phenomena, PR interval changes, ectopic beats), tachycardia cycle length regularity (irregular vs regular patterns, arrhythmia types), and P-to-QRS interval relationships (short vs long RP classification).

content.narrative_summary: Figure 1 presents a flowchart algorithm for the differential diagnosis of narrow QRS tachycardia (QRS ≤120 ms). The legend explains that retrograde P waves should be sought using a 12-lead ECG or esophageal lead; the 90 ms RP cut-off is arbitrary and based on limited data; and that the ventriculoatrial interval cut-off is 70 ms in the electrophysiology laboratory. Abbreviations AF, AT, AV, AVNRT, AVRT, JET, RP, and VT are defined.

figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Flowchart guiding diagnosis of narrow QRS tachycardia: start with narrow QRS tachycardia → assess regularity → if regular assess visible P waves → if P waves visible compare atrial vs ventricular rate → diagnose atrial flutter/Focal AT/AVNRT if atrial rate > ventricular rate; if ventricular rate > atrial rate consider high septal VT/JET/AVNRT variants or assess RP interval → with short RP (<PR, RP ≤90 ms) diagnose typical AVNRT/Focal AT/JET/AVRT; with short RP (>PR, RP >90 ms) diagnose AVRT/atypical AVNRT/Focal AT; with long RP (>PR) diagnose Focal AT/AVRT/atypical AVNRT; if not regular, consider AF or multifocal AT.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of narrow‐QRS tachycardia mechanisms, including typical AVNRT, AVRT and focal atrial tachycardia (AT), highlighting VA interval measurements, P‐wave morphology and RP interval criteria for differentiating arrhythmia types. It also describes AV block or atrioventricular dissociation during SVT, the diagnostic role of bundle branch block formation, and the impact of conduction pathways on VA interval and cycle length measurements. Section 9.1.2 introduces use of vagal manoeuvres and adenosine for clinical diagnosis when the ECG during tachycardia is unclear, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 2.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Table 8
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Possible responses of narrow QRS tachycardia to vagal manoeuvres and adenosine
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
(1) Slowing of AVN conduction and induction of intermittent AV block. Atrial electrical activity can thus be unmasked, revealing dissociated P waves (focal AT, atrial flutter, or AF waves).
(2) Temporary decrease in the atrial rate of automatic tachycardias (focal AT, sinus tachycardia, and JET).
(3) Tachycardia termination. This can happen by interrupting the re-entry circuit in AVNRT and AVRT by acting on the AVN that is part of the circuit. More rarely, sinus nodal re-entry and ATs due to triggered activity can slow down and terminate.
(4) No effect is observed in some cases.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Responses of narrow-complex tachycardias to adenosine
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
Flowchart linking responses to adenosine with diagnoses:
- No effect → Inadequate dose/delivery or high septal VT
- Gradual slowing then reacceleration → Sinus tachycardia; Automatic focal AT; Junctional ectopic tachycardia
- Sudden termination → AVNRT; AVRT; Sinus nodal re-entry; Triggered focal AT (DADs)
- Persisting atrial tachycardia with transient high-grade AV block → Atrial flutter; Micro-re-entrant focal AT
Acronyms: AT = atrial tachycardia; AV = atrioventricular; AVNRT = atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia; AVRT = atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia; DADs = delayed after-depolarizations; VT = ventricular tachycardia.

content.title: ESC Guidelines
section_headings: 10 Acute management in the absence of an established diagnosis
content.narrative_summary: Continues discussion of ECG‐based diagnostic criteria for wide QRS tachycardia, noting sensitivities of 40–80% and ~75% accuracy, reduced sensitivity in septal outflow tract regions, and the occasional need for electrophysiology study (Sect. 9.2.2). Section 9.3 defines irregular tachycardias (AF, multifocal AT, focal AT/atrial flutter), their ventricular response, and differential diagnosis of irregular wide QRS tachycardia (pre‐excited AF vs polymorphic VT). Section 10 introduces acute management of narrow QRS tachycardia without established diagnosis: initial non‐drug‐based approaches with escalation to i.v. drugs or electrical cardioversion (Figure 4). Subsections 10.1.1.1 and 10.1.1.2 describe immediate DC cardioversion for haemodynamically unstable patients and vagal manoeuvres (e.g., Valsalva) for stable patients, including reference to stimulation of the carotid receptors and effect of acetylcholine.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the acute management of narrow QRS tachycardia in the absence of an established diagnosis

rows.recommendation: Synchronized DC cardioversion is recommended for haemodynamically unstable patients.
A 12 lead ECG during tachycardia is recommended.
Vagal manoeuvres, preferably in the supine position with leg elevation, are recommended.
Adenosine (6–18 mg i.v. bolus) is recommended if vagal manoeuvres fail.
Verapamil or diltiazem (i.v.) should be considered, if vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail.
Beta-blockers (i.v. esmolol or metoprolol) should be considered if vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail.
Synchronized direct-current cardioversion is recommended when drug therapy fails to convert or control the tachycardia.

figures_tables_algorithms.summary:

- Assess haemodynamic instability: if Yes → synchronized cardioversion (Class I, Level B)

- If still ineffective → synchronized cardioversion (Class I, Level B)

content.narrative_summary: The page reviews management of wide‐QRS irregular tachycardias and introduces specific supraventricular tachycardias. It defines sinus tachycardia (>100 b.p.m.) and distinguishes physiological causes from inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST). The mechanisms of IST are discussed, including gain‐of‐function mutations in HCN4 and autoantibodies against G beta receptor. Diagnostic criteria for IST are outlined (exclusion of other causes, Holter monitoring showing mean heart rate >90 b.p.m. and exaggerated response >100 b.p.m.). section_headings: Recommendations for the therapy of sinus tachycardias
content.narrative_summary: The text discusses ivabradine metabolism via cytochrome P450 and cautions its use with CYP3A4 inhibitors and inducers. Observational data suggest catheter ablation is not routine for inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST). Medical therapy is empirical: verapamil and amiodarone have variable success, beta-blockers often ineffective; catheter ablation can be effective for sinus node re-entrant tachycardia. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is defined by heart rate increase ≥30 b.p.m. on standing, most common in young women, with ~50% spontaneous recovery; mechanisms include autonomic dysfunction and deconditioning. Diagnosis is by active stand or head-up tilt testing.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the therapy of focal atrial tachycardia

rows.recommendation: Synchronized DC cardioversion is recommended for haemodynamically unstable patients.
Adenosine (6–18 mg i.v. bolus) should be considered.
Beta-blockers (i.v. esmolol or metoprolol) should be considered in the absence of decompensated HF, if adenosine fails.
Verapamil or diltiazem (i.v.) should be considered for haemodynamically stable patients in the absence of hypotension or HFrEF, if adenosine fails.
If the above measures fail, the following may be used: i.v. ibutilide; or i.v. flecainide or propafenone; or i.v. amiodarone.

Section 12.3 introduces specific disease states, starting with atrial septal defect, noting the incidence of atrial arrhythmias and controversies regarding defect closure and risk of arrhythmia development. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the therapy of supraventricular tachycardia in congenital heart disease in adults

rows.recommendation: Anticoagulation for focal AT or atrial flutter should be similar to that for patients with AF.
Synchronized DC cardioversion is recommended for haemodynamically unstable patients.
Vagal manoeuvres, preferably in the supine position with leg elevation, are recommended.
Adenosine (6–18 mg i.v. bolus) is recommended if vagal manoeuvres fail.
i.v. verapamil or diltiazem should be considered, if vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail.
i.v. beta-blockers esmolol or metoprolol should be considered if vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail.
Synchronized DC cardioversion is recommended when drug therapy fails to convert or control the tachycardia.
Catheter ablation in experienced centres should be considered.
Beta-blockers should be considered for recurrent focal AT or atrial flutter, if ablation is not possible or successful.
In patients with SVT planned for surgical repair of a congenital heart disease anomaly, pre-operative catheter ablation or intraoperative surgical ablation should be considered.
Amiodarone may be considered for prevention if ablation is not possible or successful.
Sotalol is not recommended as a first-line antiarrhythmic drug as it is related to an increased risk of pro-arrhythmias and mortality.
Flecainide and propafenone are not recommended as first-line antiarrhythmic drugs in patients with ventricular dysfunction and severe fibrosis.

section_headings: 13 Supraventricular tachycardia in the paediatric population
content.narrative_summary: Continuing from the previous discussion of adult congenital arrhythmias, this page reviews SVTs in patients with tetralogy of Fallot, noting a high risk of supraventricular arrhythmias and recommending catheter ablation as a first-line option after evaluation for haemodynamic lesions. It then addresses atrial tachycardia in post-Fontan patients, highlighting the risk of AT, challenges of ablation, and evolving surgical and interventional modifications. Section 13 introduces paediatric SVT, emphasizing differences in cardiac maturation, electro­physiology, and drug pharmacokinetics in infants. Section 13.1 outlines detection and management of foetal arrhythmias via echocardiography and in utero drug therapy. The page concludes with the opening of section 14 on SVT in pregnancy, which is cut off.

content.narrative_summary: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) in pregnancy carries an increased risk of maternal and fetal complications, with higher incidence rates of various arrhythmias. Management prioritizes identification and treatment of underlying conditions, balancing maternal hemodynamics against fetal well-being, labor and lactation effects. Antiarrhythmic drug therapy is reserved for SVT causing hemodynamic compromise or significant symptoms; teratogenic and fetal growth risks vary by trimester, with data on many agents limited. Beta-1 selective blockers are preferred when treatment is needed beyond the first trimester.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the therapy of supraventricular tachycardia in pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Catheter ablation is recommended in symptomatic women with recurrent SVT who plan to become pregnant.
Immediate electrical cardioversion is recommended for any tachycardia with haemodynamic instability.
Vagal manoeuvres and, if these fail, adenosine are recommended for acute conversion of SVT.
An i.v. beta-1 selective beta blocker (except atenolol) should be considered for acute conversion or rate control of SVT.
i.v. digoxin in the latest pocket Gls version should be considered for rate control of AT if beta-blockers fail.
i.v. ibutilide in the latest pocket Gls version may be considered for termination of atrial flutter.
During the first trimester of pregnancy, it is recommended that all antiarrhythmic drugs should be avoided, if possible.
Beta-1 selective (except atenolol) beta-blockers or verapamil, in order of preference, should be considered for prevention of SVT in patients without WPW syndrome.
Flecainide or propafenone should be considered for prevention of SVT in patients with WPW syndrome, and without ischaemic or structural heart disease.
Flecainide or propafenone in patients without ischaemic or structural heart disease should be considered if AV nodal blocking agents fail to prevent SVT.
Digoxin or verapamil should be considered for rate control of AT if beta-blockers fail in patients without WPW syndrome.
Amiodarone is not recommended in pregnant women.
Fluoroless catheter ablation should be considered in cases of drug-refractory or poorly tolerated SVT, in experienced centres.

content.narrative_summary: This page begins with sections on electrical cardioversion and catheter ablation in pregnancy, noting that cardioversion is first-line for unstable arrhythmias and that ablation may be deferred to the second trimester but can be successful for drug-refractory SVTs. It then introduces tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (TCM), defining it as reversible LV dysfunction from persistent tachycardia or frequent ventricular ectopy, and describes its mechanism, including cellular remodeling and inflammation. The diagnosis section outlines criteria such as reduced LVEF (<30%), increased LV dimensions, use of CMR to exclude structural disease, and NT-proBNP measurements.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the therapy of supraventricular tachycardia in patients with suspected or established heart failure due to tachycardiomyopathy

rows.recommendation: Catheter ablation is recommended for TCM due to SVT.
Beta-blockers (from the list with proved mortality and morbidity benefits in HFrEF) are recommended for TCM due to SVT, when catheter ablation fails or is not applicable.
It is recommended that TCM is considered in a patient with reduced LV ejection fraction with an elevated heart rate (>100 b.p.m.).
24 h (or multiday) ambulatory ECG monitoring should be considered for diagnosis of TCM by identifying subclinical or intermittent arrhythmias.

AV nodal ablation with subsequent pacing (‘ablate and pace’), either biventricular or His-bundle pacing, is recommended if the tachycardia responsible for the TCM cannot be ablated or controlled by drugs.

content.narrative_summary: Section 16 discusses assessment and management of athletes with supraventricular arrhythmias, including evaluation for underlying disease, electrolyte imbalance, thyroid dysfunction, and stimulant use. It describes the risks of ventricular pre-excitation (WPW) in athletes, the recommendation of catheter ablation in symptomatic individuals, and risk stratification for asymptomatic athletes. It also notes that orthodromic AVRT, AVNRT, and atrial tachycardia generally have low sudden death risk but may impair performance, and that catheter ablation is preferred over β-blockers or sodium-channel blockers (which are WADA-prohibited). Section 17 introduces the limited data on arrhythmia-related motor vehicle accidents, estimated at 1–3 % of all accidents and 5–10 % of cardiac‐cause accidents.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents structured recommendation tables for the therapy of multifocal atrial tachycardia (AT), management of atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT), therapy of atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT) due to accessory pathways, acute therapy of pre-excited atrial fibrillation (AF), and the management of asymptomatic pre-excitation, detailing acute, stable, unstable, and long-term treatments with corresponding Classes of Recommendation and Levels of Evidence.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the therapy of multifocal AT

rows.recommendation: Anticoagulation as in AF is recommended for patients with atrial flutter and concomitant AF.
Synchronized DC cardioversion is recommended for haemodynamically unstable patients.
Intravenous ibutilide or i.v. or oral (in-hospital) dofetilide is recommended for conversion to sinus rhythm in the absence of QTc interval prolongation.
Low-energy (≤100 J biphasic) electrical cardioversion is recommended for conversion to sinus rhythm.
High-rate atrial pacing is recommended for termination of atrial flutter in the presence of an implanted pacemaker or defibrillator.
Catheter ablation is recommended for symptomatic, recurrent episodes of cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter.
Catheter ablation in experienced centres is recommended for symptomatic, recurrent episodes of non-CTI-dependent flutter.
Catheter ablation is recommended in patients with persistent atrial flutter or in the presence of depressed LV systolic function due to tachycardiomyopathy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the therapy of AVRT due to manifest or concealed APs

Synchronized DC cardioversion is recommended when drug therapy fails to convert or control the tachycardia.
Catheter ablation of AP(s) is recommended in patients with symptomatic, recurrent AVRT.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients with asymptomatic pre-excitation

rows.recommendation: Performance of an EPS, with the use of isoprenaline, is recommended to risk stratify individuals with asymptomatic pre-excitation who have high risk occupations/hobbies, and those who participate in competitive athletics.

Catheter ablation is recommended in asymptomatic patients in whom electrophysiology testing with the use of isoprenaline identifies high-risk properties, such as SPERRI ≤250 ms, AP ERP ≤250 ms, multiple APs, and an inducible AP-mediated tachycardia.

Catheter ablation is recommended in high-risk patients with asymptomatic pre-excitation after discussing the risks, especially of heart block associated with ablation of anteroseptal or mid-septal APs, and benefits of the procedure.
Invasive risk stratification with an EPS is recommended in patients without “low risk” characteristics at non-invasive risk stratification.

content.title: 21 Areas for further research
content.narrative_summary: Section 21 reviews advances in catheter ablation since the 1990s, including new mapping and ablation technologies (intracardiac echocardiography, robotic techniques, radiation-free labs, automated classification algorithms) and computational methods for SVT substrate characterization. It highlights emerging genetic research in SVT, describing mutations in the PRKAG2 gene linked to familial WPW syndrome and Mahaim fibres, and microdeletions in the BMP2 gene affecting cardiac conduction. Sections 22 and 23 introduce supplementary data availability and begin the author/task force member affiliations list.
